latin: Sensus gustus, ut gustus est, non solum saporabile, sed humidum percipit.
translation: The sense of taste, as taste, perceives not only what is flavourable, but also what is moist.
translation_note: 'saporabile' is the proper Aristotelian sensible quality of taste (what is capable of being tasted, i.e. flavour); the thesis claims taste also perceives an additional, non-proper quality, moisture.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch6, from Latin at farmer1998:12781

sources.text: Giles of Rome, Opera omnia III.2, p. 377
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit's proposed source, on how a person with impaired taste judges bitter and sweet differently

doctrine: Edelheit places thesis 8 among the last four Giles theses (8-11), 'focused on natural philosophy... and on the subordination of sciences' (paraphrase, edelheit2022:16745), stating: 'According to thesis 8 the sense of taste, since it is a taste, perceives not only that which has flavour, but also that which has moisture' (edelheit2022:16745). He quotes Giles's own discussion, from *Opera omnia* III.2, p. 377, of how someone whose taste is impaired ('infectum') judges bitter and sweet differently, and sometimes the reverse (paraphrase of the Latin quoted, edelheit2022:16763).
historiography: Edelheit calls the attribution to Giles of 'a very standard Aristotelian view' regarding taste 'difficult to explain' as distinctively Giles's own, drawing a parallel with thesis 11, on movement in a vacuum, which he says is 'obviously taken from Averroes commenting on Aristotle's Physics' (paraphrase, edelheit2022:16993).
